title: Solve common coding and DSA interview problems in a finance context — sliding window, two pointers, HashMap lookup, dynamic programming, and tree and graph traversal — and explain the pattern and complexity of each.
shortTitle: Coding/DSA — sliding window, two pointers, HashMap, DP, trees, graphs (finance context)

s1_definition.profdef: Data structures and algorithms (DSA) are the foundational techniques for organizing data and solving computational problems efficiently. Common patterns include the sliding window for subarray or substring problems, two pointers for sorted-array scanning, HashMap for constant-time lookup, dynamic programming for optimal substructure problems, and depth-first and breadth-first search for tree and graph traversal. Each pattern has a characteristic time and space complexity expressed in Big-O notation, and choosing the right one determines whether a solution runs in milliseconds or times out.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the back office at National Bank of India drowning in data: daily stock prices, lists of transactions, account hierarchies, and transfer networks. DSA patterns are the smart shortcuts the clerks use instead of brute force. The sliding window is like a clerk sliding a ruler across a row of daily prices to spot the best buy-and-sell window without re-reading the whole row each time. A HashMap is like an index card box where the clerk instantly finds a matching amount instead of flipping through every slip. Depth-first search is like following a chain of transfers A pays B pays C to see if the money loops back to A, which would signal money laundering.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Data structures and algorithms (DSA) are the foundational techniques for organizing data and solving computational problems efficiently. Common patterns include the sliding window for subarray or substring problems, two pointers for sorted-array scanning, HashMap for constant-time lookup, dynamic programming for optimal substructure problems, and depth-first and breadth-first search for tree and graph traversal. Each pattern has a characteristic time and space complexity expressed in Big-O notation, and choosing the right one determines whether a solution runs in milliseconds or times out.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the back office at National Bank of India drowning in data: daily stock prices, lists of transactions, account hierarchies, and transfer networks. DSA patterns are the smart shortcuts the clerks use instead of brute force. The sliding window is like a clerk sliding a ruler across a row of daily prices to spot the best buy-and-sell window without re-reading the whole row each time. A HashMap is like an index card box where the clerk instantly finds a matching amount instead of flipping through every slip. Depth-first search is like following a chain of transfers A pays B pays C to see if the money loops back to A, which would signal money laundering.

**One line to remember:** Pick the pattern that matches the problem — sliding window for subarrays, HashMap for lookups, DFS/BFS for graphs and trees, DP for optimization — and always state the time and space complexity.

sections.s2_technical:
The sliding window pattern maintains a moving range over an array and updates a running result as the window slides, which avoids recomputing from scratch. For the best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock problem, you track the minimum price seen so far and compute the profit at each day, for example `BigDecimal profit = prices[i].subtract(minPrice);` updating the maximum as you go. This runs in O(n) time and O(1) space. The same idea computes a moving average: you add the new price and subtract the one leaving the window, so each step is constant work rather than re-summing the whole window.

The HashMap pattern gives constant-time lookup, which turns many O(n squared) problems into O(n). For the two-sum problem — finding two trades that sum to a target settlement amount — you store each value's complement as you scan: `if (seen.containsKey(target - amounts[i])) return ...; seen.put(amounts[i], i);`. Each element is visited once and each lookup is O(1), so the whole thing is O(n) time and O(n) space.

Dynamic programming solves problems that have optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems by building a table from smaller answers. The coin-change problem — dispensing the minimum number of notes for an ATM withdrawal — fills a `dp[]` array where `dp[i]` is the fewest notes to make amount i, computed as `dp[i] = Math.min(dp[i], dp[i - denom] + 1)` for each denomination. This is O(amount times number of denominations) time.

Graph traversal with depth-first search detects cycles, which in finance means detecting circular transfers that can indicate money laundering. You keep a recursion stack: if you reach a node already on the current stack you have found a back-edge, which means a cycle. The code tracks two sets, one for fully visited nodes and one for the current path, and returns true the moment a node reappears in the path. This is O(V plus E) where V is accounts and E is transfers. Breadth-first search instead explores level by level using a queue, which suits account-hierarchy traversal where you want the nearest relationships first.

A senior-level nuance is to always state complexity out loud in an interview and to use money-safe types: in finance code you use BigDecimal for prices and amounts rather than double, because double loses precision. Another nuance is to handle edge cases explicitly — empty arrays, a single element, no valid answer — because interviewers watch for those.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India and its trading desk, several very different data problems show up every day, and each one maps to a classic algorithm.

Problem 1 — The trading desk has a row of daily closing prices for a stock and wants to know the maximum profit from one buy and one later sell. Scanning every pair would be slow. This is exactly the sliding-window and running-minimum pattern: track the lowest price so far and the best profit in a single pass.

Problem 2 — The settlement team has a list of trade amounts and needs to find two trades that together match a target settlement figure. Checking every pair is O(n squared). This is exactly the HashMap two-sum pattern: remember complements and find the match in one pass.

Problem 3 — The ATM team needs to dispense a withdrawal amount using the fewest notes. This is exactly the coin-change dynamic programming problem. And the fraud team needs to detect circular transfers where money loops back to its sender, which is exactly a depth-first-search cycle detection on the transfer graph.

The code contains a `MaxProfitCalculator` (sliding window and moving average), a `TwoSumFinder` (HashMap), a `CoinChangeForDenominations` (dynamic programming), and a `TransactionCycleDetector` (depth-first search), plus a test. Each class is a real, self-contained algorithm using finance data.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a price series for RELIANCE of 2200, 2350, 2100, 2450, 2400, 2550 for the max-profit algorithm; trade amounts for the two-sum; denominations 500, 200, 100 with a withdrawal amount; and a transfer graph for cycle detection.

Step 1: The max-profit algorithm starts with minPrice set to the first price 2200 and maxProfit set to zero. It then walks the remaining prices.

Step 2: At price 2350, profit is 2350 minus 2200 equals 150, which beats zero, so maxProfit becomes 150. At price 2100, the profit is negative but 2100 is a new minimum, so minPrice becomes 2100. At price 2450, profit is 2450 minus 2100 equals 350, so maxProfit becomes 350.

Step 3: At price 2400 the profit is 300, which does not beat 350. At the final price 2550, profit is 2550 minus 2100 equals 450, so maxProfit becomes 450. The algorithm returns 450, meaning buy at 2100 and sell at 2550.

Step 4: For two-sum, the finder scans amounts keeping a map of seen values. At each amount it checks whether the complement (target minus current) is already in the map; if so it returns the two indices immediately, otherwise it records the current value. This finds the matching pair in one pass.

Step 5: The coin-change dynamic program fills a dp array where dp[i] is the fewest notes for amount i, and the cycle detector runs depth-first search tracking a recursion stack so that revisiting a node currently on the stack signals a circular transfer. The test asserts the max profit is 450 and that a strictly decreasing price series yields zero profit.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ DSA PATTERNS (finance data → algorithm → result) ═══

  SLIDING WINDOW — Max Profit
    prices[2200,2350,2100,2450,2400,2550]
      │ track minPrice, maxProfit each step
      ▼
    minPrice: 2200 → 2100 ;  maxProfit: 0 → 150 → 350 → 450
      │
      ▼  O(n) time, O(1) space
    result = 450 (buy 2100, sell 2550)

  HASHMAP — Two Sum
    amounts[...] + target
      │ for each a: complement = target - a
      │ seen.containsKey(complement)? return pair : seen.put(a)
      ▼  O(n) time, O(n) space
    result = [i, j]

  DP — Coin Change (ATM)
    denominations[500,200,100], amount
      │ dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i-denom] + 1)
      ▼  O(amount × denoms)
    result = fewest notes

  DFS — Cycle Detection (fraud)
    transferGraph {SAV2001→CUR3001→ACC9001→SAV2001}
      │ visited set + recursion stack
      │ node already on stack → back-edge → cycle!
      ▼  O(V+E)
    result = true (circular transfer)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
For coding interviews I always start by identifying which pattern the problem matches, because the right pattern is the difference between an elegant linear solution and a brute-force one that times out. The core patterns I rely on are the sliding window for subarray and substring problems, the HashMap for constant-time lookup, depth-first and breadth-first search for tree and graph traversal, and dynamic programming for optimization problems with overlapping subproblems. I use finance examples because they come naturally from my work: stock prices for array problems, account hierarchies for tree traversal, and transfer networks for graph cycle detection.

For the classic best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock problem, I keep a running minimum price and compute the profit at each day, updating the maximum profit as I go, which solves it in a single O(n) pass with constant space. For finding two trades that sum to a target settlement amount, I use the HashMap two-sum approach, storing each value's complement as I scan so I find the match in one pass instead of checking every pair.

For the ATM dispensing the fewest notes, I use dynamic programming, filling a table where each entry is the minimum number of notes to make that amount, which runs in time proportional to the amount times the number of denominations. For fraud detection, I detect circular transfers using depth-first search with a recursion stack, because reaching a node that is already on the current path means there is a back-edge and therefore a cycle, which runs in time proportional to the number of accounts plus transfers.

The habits that make me look senior in an interview are stating the time and space complexity out loud for every solution, handling edge cases like empty input and no valid answer explicitly, and using BigDecimal for money rather than double so I never lose precision. In my project each algorithm is a small self-contained class with a clear single responsibility and documented complexity, which is exactly how I would structure a real trading-algorithms service so that adding a new pattern means adding one new class without touching the existing ones.
